script.opening_words: There's a 95-year-old man in Omaha, Nebraska, who still lives in the same house he bought in 1958 for $31,500. He eats breakfast at McDonald's, he drinks five Cokes a day, and he's worth roughly $150 billion. Now, here's the strange part. If you walked up to W
script.ending_words: parate times and never sold, used some of his final words as CEO to tell shareholders the same thing he'd tell you. America will come back. The math doesn't need you to be brilliant. It just needs you to stay. Thanks for watching. I'll see you in the next one.
script.analysis: Full 17201 canonical characters read. A quote-driven investing explainer that resolves an apparent paradox: Buffett's two answers (index fund for most people versus 50% a year on small sums). Structure: hook with the Omaha-house paradox, will instruction, the Protégé bet, debt-first rule, cash, index compounding math, behaviour gap (DALBAR, best-days), fees, then the 1999 "50% a year" claim, his early methods (GEICO, Moody's manual, Korean stocks), why size ends it, 2026 valuation context, and a one-breath recap. Strong throughline and a payoff that dissolves the paradox ("the same answer applied to two different people"). Weaknesses: the bet's dollar figures ($220,000 versus "854 dollars") and the "2.2% per year" are contradicted by the Berkshire table; "first time in almost two decades" is contradicted by 2023-24 data; the fee gap of $18,000 holds only near 7%, not the script's 10%; several quotes and statistics (2020 meeting, 2024 meeting, partnership results, Berkshire cash, DALBAR, J.P. Morgan) are recall or secondary corroboration only. Early subscribe ask before the first payoff. One sponsor-free outro.
beat_map: Hook: 95-year-old Omaha billionaire, $31,500 house, McDonald's breakfast; "he would tell you not to pick stocks" yet could earn hedge-fund-beating returns on $10,000; both true.
Promise and framing: "which of his two answers belongs to you"; disclaimer; early subscribe request; public answer versus personal answer.
Public answer: 2013 letter will instruction, 10% short-term government bonds and 90% low-cost S&P 500 index fund.
Evidence: 2008 Protégé bet, 125.8% versus hedge-fund funds; dollar illustration; "the index is the trophy".
Precondition: pay off 18%/24% credit-card debt first ("I don't know how to make 18%").
Cash you can reach: emergency fund, "boring cash finally pays", 4-5% savings, Treasury bills.
The index answer in numbers: 10% a year gives $26,000 / $67,000 / $174,000 / $452,000 over 10 to 40 years.
Behaviour gap: DALBAR 2024 25% versus 16.5%; missing 10 best days; seven of best days near worst days; fees $18,000.
Pivot: "here's where this video earns its title" - the 1999 "50% a year on $1 million" guarantee and compounding to $576,000 / $33 million.
Why not recommend it: what young Buffett actually did (GEICO train trip, Moody's manual, Western Insurance, National American Fire, partnership 1957-69).
Size limits returns: Berkshire cash pile, "no possibility of eye-popping performance", Korean stocks 2004.
2026 context: Buffett steps down as CEO, Abel, final letter, Shiller PE 40.7, Berkshire sits on cash.
Resolution: do not time the market; dollar-cost averaging into an index fund; the two answers are the same answer for two kinds of people.
Recap in one breath: kill 18% debt, emergency fund, 90/10, add monthly, do nothing; median $8,000 household; "America will come back"; close.

claim_audit.claim: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. I suggest Vanguard's.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Put 10% of the cash in
short-term government bonds and 90% in a
very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. I

claim_audit.assessment: [PRIMARY_SOURCE_DIRECTLY_INSPECTED] Berkshire 2013 shareholder letter (PDF text layer, SHA-256 in receipt): "Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. (I suggest Vanguard's.)" It is an instruction to the trustee for his wife's cash bequest, which the letter says mirrors his will. Quote matches; the video's "the one he wrote into his own will" is a fair paraphrase.

claim_audit.claim: A million dollars in the hedge funds gained about $220,000. The same million in the index fund gained 854 dollars.
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
A million
dollars in the hedge funds gained about
$220,000.
The same million in the index fund
gained 854
dollars.
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] Contradicted by the letter table. $1 million at the 125.8% index gain gained about $1,258,000; at the five-fund mean final gain of 36.3% it gained about $363,000 (about $243,000 only if 2.2% per year were right). $220,000 matches simple 2.2% x 10 years, not compounding. "$854" matches nothing in the table and is irreconcilable with 125.8%; the sentence inverts the true ordering magnitude (index gain was about 3.5x the hedge-fund basket). Likely a script or narration error.
